slides.title: Existence of a solution
slides.text:
Existence of a solution

•  Workspace is that volume of space which the end-
   effector of the manipulator can reach.
•  For a solution to exist the specified goal point must lie
   within the workspace.
•  Dextrous workspace is that volume of space which the
   robot end-effector can reach with all orientations.
•  Reachable work space is that volume of space which the
   robot can reach in atleast one orientation.
•  For a two-link manipulator
   –  If 𝐿1 = 𝐿2, reachable work space is a disc of radius
       2𝐿1; the dextrous workspace is a point: origin.
   –  If 𝐿1 ≠𝐿2, there is no dextrous workspace. The
       reachable workspace is a ring of outer radius 𝐿1 + 𝐿2
      and inner radius 𝐿1 −𝐿2.


                                                                                                           7

visualInspection.notes: Printed 7; reachable vs dextrous; equal two-link disk radius 2L and dextrous origin. Unequal annulus printed inner L1-L2 requires ordering or absolute value; no joint limits assumed.

slides.title: Multiple solutions
slides.text:
Multiple solutions

•  The inverse kinematic problem may have more than
   one solution.
•  For a given problem, we need to calculate all the
   possible solutions.
•  The system must be able to choose one solution.                                                         Normally not preferred as
•  A good solution is one that requires each joint to           it requires large joint
   have minimal rotation.                                                            angle movements, if
•    If an obstacle is present, then another solution can     obstacle then yes.
   be chosen.
•  For PUMA 560, there can be eight solutions for a
   single goal.
•   In general, more non zero link parameters there are,
   the more ways there will be to reach a certain goal.



                                                                                                           8

visualInspection.notes: Printed 8; alternate elbow configurations and obstacle figure; prefer smaller joint motion absent collision. PUMA example can have eight, not always.

slides.title: Some Useful Definition
slides.text:
Some Useful Definition

•  Linear: A function 𝑓 is linear if it satisfies two axioms: additivity
  𝑓𝑥+ 𝑦= 𝑓𝑥+ 𝑓(𝑦) and homogeneity 𝑓𝛼𝑥= 𝛼𝑥  for scalar
   𝛼. This superposition principle allows complex problems to be broken
   into simpler linear parts, common in robotics and AI signal processing.
•  Solvable: Has a unique solution.
•  Closed Form: Can be computed Algebraically and provides all solutions.
•  Numerical: Iterative Process.
•  Algebraic: Uses algebraic identities to substitute and to solve.
•  Geometric: Utilizes geometric relationships, law of
   cosines, etc
•  Sub-Space: Smaller Region; Circle in a plane
   Sphere in XYZ space

visualInspection.notes: Printed 10; definitions. Homogeneity misprint f(alpha x)=alpha x. Solvable defined unique contradicts later pages. Circle/sphere called subspaces but not linear subspaces generally.

slides.title: Method of solution
slides.text:
Method of solution

•  Manipulator equations are non-linear, so we do not have a general
  method to solve these equations.
•   All systems with revolute and prismatic joints having a total of 6 DOF in a
   single series chain are solvable.
•  However, this general solution is numerical.
•  Robots with analytical solution have several intersecting joint axes
   and/or many 𝛼𝑖= 0, 90°.
•  A manipulator is solvable if the joint variables can be
   found by an algorithm.
•  The algorithm should find all possible
   joint variables associated with given position and
   orientation.



                                                                                                          11

visualInspection.notes: Printed 11; nonlinear/transcendental equations; algorithmic definition of solvable and all branches. Broad solvability claims require reachable targets and convergence qualifications.

slides.title: Main Methods
slides.text:
Main Methods

•  Numerical
   –  Iterative
•  Closed Form
   –  Algebraic
   – Geometric
• We prefer an analytical solution over a numerical one, as numerical
   solutions are time-consuming.
•  A sufficient condition that a manipulator with 6
   revolute joints will have a closed-form solution
    is that three neighbouring joint axes intersect at
   a point.



                                                                                                          12

visualInspection.notes: Printed 12; numerical versus closed form; sufficient condition three neighboring axes intersect at point in 6R.

slides.title: Kinematics
slides.text:
Kinematics

•   Kinematics can play a large role in both the computational
   requirements for the robot, and in its range of motion.
•  Most industrial robots have simple kinematics to reduce
   computational burden, often they have spherical wrists.
•  A spherical wrist is a three-joint robotic end-effector design (typically
    joints 4-6 in a 6-DOF manipulator) where the three joint axes intersect
    at a single common point, creating a spherical motion envelope.
•  Almost always have 3 intersecting axes.
    –  Pieper’s Solution guarantees a closed form inverse kinematic
        solution.
•   Sine and Cosine terms handled in look-up table.
    – We can store both the sine and cosine in one table.
    – Need only one forth of the full table.



                                                                                                          13

visualInspection.notes: Printed 13; spherical wrist joints4,5,6 common intersection; Pieper solution; quarter-wave sine/cosine lookup.

slides.title: Summary
slides.text:
Summary

•  IK is the inverse problem of FK: Find joint configs that achieve a
   desired end-effector pose.
•  Analytical IK: Closed-form, fast, but limited to specific robot
   geometries.
•  Numerical IK: Jacobian-based methods work generally but need
   singularity handling.
• Wheeled Robot IK: Diff-drive – find individual
  wheel angular velocities (𝑢𝑙, 𝑢𝑟) given the
  motion (𝑣, 𝜔) of the robot.



                                                                                                          25

visualInspection.notes: Printed 25. Summary repeats IK/analytical/wheel roles but adds explicit numerical Jacobian singularity-handling caution; retain examinable rather than purely repeated.

visualInspection.notes: Printed 27. Thank You only.

sourceIssues.finding: Unequal-link inner radius printed L1-L2 without length-order assumption.
sourceIssues.handling: Questions use |L1-L2| explicitly or state L1>=L2.2R workspace claims are bounded to planar unrestricted joints without obstacles.

sourceIssues.finding: Solution-count table lacks detailed geometric hypotheses; prose suggests strictly more solutions with more nonzero lengths despite two equal<=16 rows.
sourceIssues.handling: Ask source-attributed row bounds and distinguish maximum from exact count, not a universal theorem about arbitrary6R geometry.

sourceIssues.finding: Printed f(alpha x)=alpha x omits f on the right; fails e.g. f(x)=2x.
sourceIssues.handling: Questions explicitly request repaired f(alpha x)=alpha f(x), with exact counterexample.

sourceIssues.finding: Solvable=unique contradicts multi-solution and later algorithmic definition; circles/spheres as subspaces conflates arbitrary subsets with linear vector subspaces.
sourceIssues.handling: Question contrasts definitions explicitly; unit-circle closure counterexample is supplied, not treated as a source fact.

sourceIssues.finding: Broad all6DOF serial systems solvable/general numerical wording cannot guarantee reachable targets, convergence, uniqueness or all branches from a single initial guess.
sourceIssues.handling: State reachable target, branch enumeration and algorithm limitations; no unconditional numerical guarantee.

sourceIssues.finding: Text says c2 outside[-1,1] means too far away; c2<-1 actually identifies an inner unreachable region.
sourceIssues.handling: Derive both triangle inequalities and supply separate too-close and too-far numerical counterexamples.

sourceIssues.finding: Visible middle x/r line uses cos(gamma)cos(theta1)-sin(gamma)cos(theta1), repeating cos(theta1).
sourceIssues.handling: Explicit repair changes the final factor to sin(theta1); derive from correct upper equations and verify forward roundtrips.

sourceIssues.finding: Origin arbitrary theta1 omits equal-positive-link reachability condition and principal-angle modulo qualification.
sourceIssues.handling: State equal lengths and folded elbow for the continuous origin family; never use atan2(0,0) software output as a physical constraint.

sourceIssues.finding: Only upper triangle inequality is printed; claim that a triangle exists only for negative elbow range conflicts with the explicitly given reflected branch.
sourceIssues.handling: Use lower and upper bounds; treat negative elbow interval as the pictured branch convention, not the only physical branch.

sourceIssues.finding: Final line visibly prints theta3=phi-theta1+theta2, inconsistent with preceding theta1+theta2+theta3=phi.
sourceIssues.handling: Explicitly repair to phi-theta1-theta2 and test both position and orientation; preserve defective line in citation evidence.

sourceIssues.finding: Main J^-1 notation attempts ordinary inversion of3x2J. Flow drawing labels qdot->J->pdot and pdot->J^-1->qdot, swapped relative to qdot=Jpdot.
sourceIssues.handling: Explicitly distinguish source drawing from corrected input/output dimensions. Use next-page pseudoinverse with feasibility assumptions.

sourceIssues.finding: Full-rank shortcut is valid only for its stated rank case. A3x2 Jacobian does not realize arbitrary3-component desired rates; source does not discuss incompatible lateral targets.
sourceIssues.handling: Derive no-lateral constraint and projection; distinguish least-squares output from exact physical realization and singular shortcut from general pseudoinverse.
